Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems

Nicolas Zilberstein Affiliation: Rice University Email: nzilberstein@rice.edu    Morteza Mardani Affiliation: NVIDIA Inc. Email: mmardani@nvidia.com    Santiago Segarra Affiliation: Rice University Email: segarra@rice.edu
Abstract

Image restoration faces a fundamental tradeoff: methods that minimize error produce blurry reconstructions, while those that maximize perceptual quality yield sharp but less faithful images. Existing approaches either commit to a single operating point on this distortion perception (DP) frontier or require paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning of the sampler to access different points. We show that flow map models, a recent extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average field, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers that continuously spans the DP frontier. The lookahead parameter t acts as a control knob between the MMSE and perceptual regimes. For Gaussian targets, we prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier; for natural images, we observe similar behavior empirically. Within a Plug-and-Play solver, the same mechanism extends to general inverse problems, where it controls a tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency. Despite the lack of exact optimality guarantees in this setting, a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes. Extensive experiments on CelebA (128×128128\times 128) and AFHQ (256×256256\times 256) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate our findings. Code is available in https://github.com/nzilberstein/Flow-map-denoisers

1 Introduction

Image restoration is a highly ill-posed inverse problem: a single degraded observation can correspond to a vast set of plausible clean images. Standard regression approaches that minimize mean squared error (MSE) approximate the conditional expectation (Ongie et al., 2020), achieving minimum distortion at the cost of over-smoothed reconstructions that lack fine detail. In contrast, posterior sampling techniques (Kawar et al., 2021) produce realistic-looking solutions at the cost of higher distortion. This inherent compromise is formalized by the distortion-perception (DP) tradeoff (Blau and Michaeli, 2018; Freirich et al., 2021). Because the ideal balance between low distortion and high perceptual quality is strictly user-dependent, designing a single model capable of traversing the DP plane at inference time remains a central challenge in computational imaging.

Most existing methods commit to a single operating point in the DP plane, either targeting minimum distortion through supervised regression (Dong et al., 2015; Terris et al., 2026), or minimum perception by leveraging recent generative models as priors (Pokle et al., 2024; Chung et al., 2023; Kadkhodaie and Simoncelli, 2021) to draw samples from the posterior. A few recent works based on data-dependent flow models aim to traverse the DP plane (Ohayon et al., 2025; Delbracio and Milanfar, 2023; Albergo et al., 2024), by explicitly interpolating between measurement-dependent estimators (e.g., the conditional mean) and the clean image. Unlike these approaches, which require external mechanisms, such as interpolation, discretization choices, or retraining, to move along the DP frontier, we show that this tradeoff is already implicitly encoded in the dynamics of flow maps.

This raises the question of whether this behavior can be achieved without relying on solver choices, such as increasing the number of discretization steps. In this work, we propose a unified approach based on flow maps (Boffi et al., 2025b; Boffi et al., 2025a; Geng et al., 2025; Sabour et al., 2025b), which unifies all operating points along the DP plane within a single model. While prior work primarily uses flow maps to accelerate sampling (Gülle et al., 2026; Sabour et al., 2025a; Spagnoletti et al., 2025), we instead leverage them to traverse the DP frontier. Our key observation is that the lookahead tt selects a point along a continuum of estimators—termed average denoisers—implicitly encoded within a single trained flow map, thus acting as a knob to control the characteristics of the restored image. This perspective reveals DP control as an intrinsic property of the learned flow map, eliminating the need for multiple models, auxiliary networks, or heuristic solver choices.

This family spans the entire DP frontier, recovering the MMSE estimator at one extreme and approaching posterior sampling at the other. For Gaussian targets, we prove that this family spans the entire DP frontier, recovering the MMSE estimator at one extreme and approaching posterior sampling at the other, tracing the optimal DP curve (Freirich et al., 2021). While this exact theoretical correspondence strictly holds for Gaussian noise problems, we empirically observe similar behavior for natural images. When extending this approach to general, non-Gaussian inverse problems, traversing the lookahead serves as an approximation to the true DP frontier; here, the lookahead controls a tradeoff that combines perceptual alignment with data-consistency effects, rather than exactly reproducing the denoising DP frontier. By embedding these denoisers within a Plug-and-Play (PnP) framework (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2013), we leverage this property to obtain a versatile solver that effectively traverses the DP frontier across a wide range of inverse problems. Fig. 1 illustrates this behavior on a 2D Gaussian mixture model.

Overall, our contributions are:

  • •

    Flow maps as a continuum of DP estimators. We reinterpret flow maps as a family of denoisers indexed by a lookahead parameter tt, enabling continuous traversal of the DP plane with a single model.

  • •

    Exact optimality in the Gaussian case. We show that this family recovers the optimal DP curve for Gaussian targets, establishing a direct link between flow maps and DP theory.

  • •

    PnP reconstruction with continuous control. We embed these denoisers into a plug-and-play framework, yielding a unified solver that spans the entire DP plane without retraining, and enables high-perceptual reconstructions at a fraction of the cost of posterior sampling methods.

  • •

    Empirical validation. On CelebA and AFHQ inverse problems (inpainting, motion deblurring, super-resolution, Gaussian deblurring), our method matches or exceeds specialized baselines at both DP endpoints from a single trained model, and uniquely traces a smooth DP curve in between.

Notation.

Bold symbols (e.g., 𝐱\mathbf{x}) denote vectors, and bold uppercase symbols (e.g., 𝐇\mathbf{H}) denote matrices. Mappings such as the flow map Xs,tX_{s,t} and denoisers Ds,tD_{s,t} are written in standard (non-bold) font.

2 Background

2.1 Flow matching and flow maps

Stochastic interpolants.

Stochastic interpolants (Albergo et al., 2025; Lipman et al., 2023) define a family of stochastic processes that interpolate between a source distribution p0p_{0} (typically 𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})) and a target distribution p1p_{1} (the data distribution):

𝐱t=αt​𝐱0+βt​𝐱1,{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=\alpha_{t}{\mathbf{x}}_{0}+\beta_{t}{\mathbf{x}}_{1}, (1)

where α,β:[0,1]→ℝ\alpha,\beta:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} are continuously differentiable functions satisfying the boundary conditions α0=1,α1=0\alpha_{0}=1,\alpha_{1}=0 and β0=0,β1=1\beta_{0}=0,\beta_{1}=1. A common choice is the linear interpolant αt=1−t\alpha_{t}=1-t and βt=t\beta_{t}=t, yielding 𝐱t=(1−t)​𝐱0+t​𝐱1{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=(1-t){\mathbf{x}}_{0}+t{\mathbf{x}}_{1}. The marginal velocity field 𝐯⁡(𝐱,t)=𝔼⁡[𝐱˙t∣𝐱t=𝐱]{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t)=\mathbb{E}[\dot{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{t}={\mathbf{x}}] yields an ODE 𝐱˙t=𝐯t​(𝐱t)\dot{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t}={\mathbf{v}}_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{t}), defining a continuous-time transport map from the source to the target distribution and which can be used to draw samples from p1p_{1}. In practice, a neural network 𝐯θ​(𝐱,t){\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}},t) is trained to approximate vtv_{t} via the mean square error loss:

𝔼t,𝐱0,𝐱1​[‖𝐯θ​(𝐱t,t)−(α˙t​𝐱0+β˙t​𝐱1)‖22],\mathbb{E}_{t,{\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{x}}_{1}}\left[\left\|{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)-(\dot{\alpha}_{t}{\mathbf{x}}_{0}+\dot{\beta}_{t}{\mathbf{x}}_{1})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (2)

which plays a role analogous to denoising score matching Vincent (2011) in diffusion models Song et al. (2021). For the linear interpolant, the velocity field relates directly to the Minimum Mean Squared Error (MMSE) denoiser – instantaneous denoiser – via Tweedie’s formula (Robbins, 1956; Miyasawa and others, 1961):

Dt​(𝐱):=𝔼⁡[𝐱1∣𝐱t=𝐱]=𝐱+(1−t)​𝐯​(𝐱,t).D_{t}({\mathbf{x}}):=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{t}={\mathbf{x}}]={\mathbf{x}}+(1-t){\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t). (3)

A detailed characterization of denoisers can be found in (Milanfar and Delbracio, 2025).

Flow maps.

Sampling from p1p_{1} using the learned velocity field requires numerical integration of the ODE, typically with many function evaluations. Flow maps (Boffi et al., 2025b; Boffi et al., 2025a; Geng et al., 2025) bypass this integration by training a model to directly predict the average over a finite interval [s,t][s,t]:

Xs,t​(𝐱)=𝐱+(t−s)​𝐯​(𝐱,s,t),X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{x}}+(t-s)\,{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},s,t), (4)

where 𝐯⁡(𝐱,s,t){\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},s,t) is the average velocity over the interval [s,t][s,t]. A network vθ​(x,s,t)v_{\theta}(x,s,t) is trained to predict this average velocity, conditioned on both the current time ss and the target time tt. While there are different alternatives for the loss for training flow maps Boffi et al. (2025b), in this work we consider the Lagrangian self-distillation (LSD) given by

ℒLSD​(v^)=∫01∫0t𝔼𝐱0,𝐱1​[‖∂tX^s,t​(𝐱s)−𝐯θ​(X^s,t​(𝐱s),t)‖2]​𝑑s​𝑑t.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LSD}}(\hat{v})=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{x}}_{1}}\left[\left\|\partial_{t}\hat{X}_{s,t}\left({\mathbf{x}}_{s}\right)-{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}\left(\hat{X}_{s,t}\left({\mathbf{x}}_{s}\right),t\right)\right\|^{2}\right]d\mathrm{s}d\mathrm{t}. (5)

We consider the LSD as it achieved the most stable training in practice and a good visual result; we include further background in Appendix A.1.

2.2 Inverse problems and Plug-and-Play methods

We consider inverse problems of the form

𝐲=f⁡(𝐱)+𝐯,{\mathbf{y}}=f({\mathbf{x}})+{\mathbf{v}}, (6)

where f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) is a known (possibly non-linear) degradation operator and 𝐯{\mathbf{v}} is an additive noise, typically Gaussian 𝐯∼𝒩⁡(0,σ​𝐈){\mathbf{v}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma{\mathbf{I}}). Two main families of methods combine flow or diffusion priors with data-consistency updates (Daras et al., 2024; Chung et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025): guidance-based methods (Zhang et al., 2024; Pokle et al., 2024; Chung et al., 2023; Song et al., 2022) and plug-and-play (optimization-based) methods (Ben-Hamu et al., 2024; Martin et al., 2025). We focus on the latter and defer a discussion of guidance-based approaches to Appendix A.2.

Plug-and-Play methods.

Plug-and-Play (PnP) algorithms (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2013; Romano et al., 2017) originate from proximal optimization methods for solving inverse problems of the form min𝐱⁡g⁡(𝐱)+h⁡(𝐱)\min_{\mathbf{x}}g({\mathbf{x}})+h({\mathbf{x}}). In particular, forward–backward splitting (FBS) alternates between a gradient step on the data-fidelity term and a proximal step on the regularizer:

𝐳k\displaystyle{\mathbf{z}}^{k} =𝐱k−λt∇g(𝐱k),\displaystyle={\mathbf{x}}^{k}-\lambda_{t}\nabla g({\mathbf{x}}^{k}), (7)
𝐱k+1\displaystyle{\mathbf{x}}^{k+1} =proxλ​h​(𝐳k),\displaystyle=\mathrm{prox}_{\lambda h}({\mathbf{z}}^{k}), (8)

where the proximal operator is defined as proxλ​h​(𝐳):=arg⁡min𝐱​12​‖𝐱−𝐳‖2+λ​h​(𝐱)\mathrm{prox}_{\lambda h}({\mathbf{z}}):=\arg\min_{{\mathbf{x}}}\tfrac{1}{2}\|{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{z}}\|^{2}+\lambda h({\mathbf{x}}). Computing proxλ​h\mathrm{prox}_{\lambda h} corresponds to solving a denoising problem.

Flow and diffusion models as PnP priors.

Recent works instantiate this proximal step with a learned denoiser DtD_{t}, yielding the iteration 𝐱k+1=Dt​(𝐳k){\mathbf{x}}^{k+1}=D_{t}({\mathbf{z}}^{k}) (Zhu et al., 2023; Martin et al., 2025; Mardani et al., 2024; Zilberstein et al., 2025; Renaud et al., 2024; Laumont et al., 2022; Laumont et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024). This approach leverages implicit priors learned by generative models while retaining the flexibility of PnP for arbitrary forward operators. However, these methods typically optimize distortion, often at the expense of perceptual quality, resulting in over-smoothed reconstructions. In Section 3, we show that replacing the instantaneous denoiser with an average denoiser associated to the flow-map enables continuous control over this tradeoff and improves perceptual quality.

2.3 Distortion-Perception Tradeoff

The standard evaluation of image restoration methods relies on average distortion D=𝔼⁡[Δ⁡(𝐱,𝐱^)]D=\mathbb{E}[\Delta({\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}})] (e.g., MSE or LPIPS), which measures the discrepancy between the ground truth 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} and its estimate 𝐱^\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}. However, since reconstructions should also appear natural to humans, methods are additionally assessed by perceptual quality. In practice, this is approximated by a perceptual index P=d⁡(p𝐱,p𝐱^)P=d(p_{\mathbf{x}},p_{\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}}), measuring the divergence (e.g., Wasserstein distance) between the true and reconstructed distributions, and estimated via surrogates such as FID (Heusel et al., 2017) or KID (Bińkowski et al., 2018).

Blau and Michaeli (2018) showed that distortion and perception are fundamentally at odds, defining the distortion–perception (DP) tradeoff. Formally, the DP function is

D⁡(P)=minp𝐱^|𝐲⁡𝔼⁡[‖𝐱−𝐱^‖]s.t.W2​(p𝐱,p𝐱^)≤P,D(P)=\min_{p_{\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}|{\mathbf{y}}}}\mathbb{E}[\|{\mathbf{x}}-\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}\|]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad W_{2}(p_{\mathbf{x}},p_{\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}})\leq P,

where we considered the MSE distortion and Wasserstein distance for perception. For this choice, Freirich et al. (2021) showed that the optimal curve is D⁡(P)=D∗+max⁡{(P∗−P)2,0},P∈[0,P∗]D(P)=D^{*}+\max\{(P^{*}-P)^{2},0\},\quad P\in[0,P^{*}], where D∗=𝔼⁡[‖𝐱−𝐱∗‖2]D^{*}=\mathbb{E}[\|{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{x}}^{*}\|^{2}] is the MMSE distortion and P∗=W2​(p𝐱,p𝐱∗)P^{*}=W_{2}(p_{\mathbf{x}},p_{{\mathbf{x}}^{*}}) is the perceptual gap of the posterior mean 𝐱∗=𝔼⁡[𝐱|𝐲]{\mathbf{x}}^{*}=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}|{\mathbf{y}}]. The optimal estimator at each perception level is given by the interpolation

𝐱^P=(1−PP∗)​𝐱^0+PP∗​𝐱∗,\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{P}=\left(1-\frac{P}{P^{*}}\right)\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}+\frac{P}{P^{*}}{\mathbf{x}}^{*}, (9)

where 𝐱^0\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0} is a perfectly perceptual estimator. This result implies that the entire DP frontier can be recovered by interpolating between two endpoints: the MMSE estimator 𝐱∗{\mathbf{x}}^{*} and a perceptually optimal estimator 𝐱^0\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}. However, existing approaches require explicit interpolation between multiple models or task-specific retraining to access different operating points (Delbracio and Milanfar, 2023; Ohayon et al., 2025). In contrast, we seek a single model that directly parameterizes this continuum, enabling continuous traversal of the DP plane.

3 Average denoisers: traversing the DP plane

In this section we define and analyze the average denoiser associated to flow maps and its connection to the DP tradeoff (Section 3.1).

3.1 Flow maps as denoisers

Recall we seek a family of estimators parametrized by a single model that interpolates between P∗P^{*} (lowest distortion) and P=0P=0 (lowest perception). A natural candidate is the denoiser implicitly defined by the flow map (Section 2.1). The same object was independently introduced by Lee et al. (2026) for one-step language modeling on discrete data; here we study it in the continuous setting and show it parametrizes the DP frontier.

Definition 1 (Average denoiser)

Given a flow map with average velocity 𝐯(.,s,t){\mathbf{v}}(.,s,t), the average denoiser (or two-time denoiser) is:

Ds,t​(𝐱):=𝐱+(1−s)​𝐯​(𝐱,s,t).D_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}}):={\mathbf{x}}+(1-s){\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},s,t). (10)

This definition has the same form as the instantaneous denoiser (3), but replaces the instantaneous velocity 𝐯(.,s){\mathbf{v}}(.,s) with the average velocity 𝐯(.,s,t){\mathbf{v}}(.,s,t) over the interval [s,t][s,t]. This modification has an important consequence: the parameter tt now controls where Ds,t​(𝐱)D_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}}) sits on the DP plane, i.e., varying tt traces a continuous path between the low-distortion and low-perception extremes. Importantly, both ss and tt are inputs of 𝐯θ​(𝐱,s,t){\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},s,t), so a single trained model produces a whole family of denoisers with different characteristics, as we show in the following section.

3.2 Traversing the DP plane with flow maps

3.2.1 Warm-up: Gaussian case (1D analysis)

We start with the Gaussian case, which renders a closed-form expression of the average denoiser in (10). For clarity, we derive the results in the scalar case (x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}); all results extend directly to the multivariate setting by applying the analysis component-wise. Let p1=𝒩⁡(0,σp2)p_{1}={\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma_{p}^{2}), with σp2≤1\sigma_{p}^{2}\leq 1; following the stochastic interpolant formulation in Section 2.1, the marginal variance at noise level tt is σt2=t2​σp2+(1−t)2\sigma_{t}^{2}=t^{2}\sigma_{p}^{2}+(1-t)^{2}, and the instantaneous denoiser is linear, given by 𝔼⁡[x1∣xt=x]=At​x\mathbb{E}[x_{1}\mid x_{t}=x]=A_{t}x, with At=t​σp2/σt2A_{t}=t\sigma_{p}^{2}/\sigma_{t}^{2}. Using Tweedie’s relationship in (3), we also have a linear instantaneous velocity field v⁡(x,t)=Bt​xv(x,t)=B_{t}x with Bt=[t⁡(σp2+1)−1]/σt2B_{t}=[t(\sigma_{p}^{2}+1)-1]/\sigma_{t}^{2}.

Flow map and average denoiser.

The linearity of the instantaneous velocity yields a scalar flow map xt=Φ⁡(t,s)​xsx_{t}=\Phi(t,s)\,x_{s} with Φ⁡(t,s)=σt/σs\Phi(t,s)=\sigma_{t}/\sigma_{s}, obtained by integrating ∫stBτ​𝑑τ=log⁡(σt/σs)\int_{s}^{t}B_{\tau}\,d\tau=\log(\sigma_{t}/\sigma_{s}) (see Appendix D.2). Following Definition 1, the average denoiser reduces to Ds,t​(xs)=Λ⁡(s,t)​xsD_{s,t}(x_{s})=\Lambda(s,t)\,x_{s} where:

Λ⁡(s,t)=(1−s)​σt−(1−t)​σsσs​(t−s).\Lambda(s,t)=\frac{(1-s)\sigma_{t}-(1-t)\sigma_{s}}{\sigma_{s}(t-s)}. (11)

This gain satisfies Λ⁡(s,s)=As\Lambda(s,s)=A_{s} (lowest distortion) and Λ⁡(s,1)=σp/σs\Lambda(s,1)=\sigma_{p}/\sigma_{s} (lowest perception), and is strictly increasing in tt (see Appendix D.2).

Optimal DP estimators in the Gaussian case.

For a Gaussian target, the optimal DP estimator in (9) is also linear, given by x^P=Γ⁡(α)​xs\hat{x}_{P}=\Gamma(\alpha)\,x_{s}, with the gain given by

Γ⁡(α)=α​As+(1−α)​σp/σs.\Gamma(\alpha)=\alpha\,A_{s}+(1-\alpha)\,\sigma_{p}/\sigma_{s}. (12)

The parameter α=P/P∗∈[0,1]\alpha=P/P^{*}\in[0,1] parametrizes the perception level, interpolating linearly between the MMSE gain AsA_{s} and the best perception gain σp/σs\sigma_{p}/\sigma_{s}. Given this particular instance of the DP estimator, we can establish a direct relationship between the flow map and the DP estimator in the Gaussian case:

Theorem 1 (Exact optimality)

Let p1=𝒩⁡(0,σp2)p_{1}=\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{p}^{2}) with σp2≤1\sigma_{p}^{2}\leq 1, and let Λ⁡(s,t)\Lambda(s,t) be the average denoiser gain (11) associated with the true flow map. Then for every s∈(0,1)s\in(0,1) and t∈[s,1]t\in[s,1], there exists a perception level

α⁡(s,t)=σp/σs−Λ⁡(s,t)σp/σs−As∈[0,1]\alpha(s,t)=\frac{\sigma_{p}/\sigma_{s}-\Lambda(s,t)}{\sigma_{p}/\sigma_{s}-A_{s}}\in[0,1] (13)

such that Λ⁡(s,t)=Γ⁡(α⁡(s,t))\Lambda(s,t)=\Gamma(\alpha(s,t)). Moreover, α⁡(s,t)\alpha(s,t) decreases monotonically from 11 at t=st=s (MMSE, P=P∗P=P^{*}) to 00 at t=1t=1 (perfect perception, P=0P=0). Consequently, the average denoiser Ds,tD_{s,t} traces the optimal DP curve exactly as tt varies in [s,1][s,1].

The proof is deferred to Appendix D.2. In summary, both Λ⁡(s,t)\Lambda(s,t) and the optimal DP gain Γ⁡(α)\Gamma(\alpha) are continuous monotonic functions that share the same endpoints: AsA_{s} (MMSE, lowest distortion) and σp/σs\sigma_{p}/\sigma_{s} (lowest perception). Hence, inverting the affine relation Γ⁡(α)=Λ⁡(s,t)\Gamma(\alpha)=\Lambda(s,t) yields a bijection α⁡(s,t)\alpha(s,t) between the lookahead and the perception level, so the average denoiser exactly realizes the optimal DP estimator at every intermediate operating point. We now extend this insight to more general distributions.

3.3 Beyond the Gaussian case: image denoising experiments

For general image distributions, the average denoiser no longer admits a closed-form characterization. While exact DP optimality is not expected beyond the Gaussian case, the structural insight underlying Theorem 1 should still hold: as tt varies from ss to 11, the output of Ds,tD_{s,t} is expected to interpolate smoothly between the MMSE estimator (low distortion, low perception quality) and a perceptually-aligned estimator (higher distortion, improved perception). Consequently, we expect (i)(i) smooth, monotonic DP curves parameterized by tt, and (i​i)(ii) convex trajectories consistent with the optimal DP function (Section 2.3), which we verify empirically below. While this section focuses on image data, we further support this intuition for a 2D mixture of Gaussians (MoG) in Appendix D.3, where the DP curve can be computed explicitly.

Setup.

We train a flow map network 𝐯θ​(𝐱,s,t){\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}},s,t) on CelebA 128×128128\times 128 (Appendix B) and evaluate Ds,t​(𝐱s)D_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}}_{s}) at multiple lookahead values t∈[s,1]t\in[s,1], where t=st=s recovers the MMSE denoiser DsD_{s} and t=1t=1 reaches the endpoint of the flow. Since the stochastic interpolant (1) at time ss takes the form 𝐱s=s​𝐱1+(1−s)​ϵ{\mathbf{x}}_{s}=s\,{\mathbf{x}}_{1}+(1-s)\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon} with ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}), applying the average denoiser Ds,tD_{s,t} to 𝐱s{\mathbf{x}}_{s} corresponds to Gaussian denoising: recovering the clean signal 𝐱1{\mathbf{x}}_{1} from an observation where the signal is scaled by ss and corrupted by noise of standard deviation 1−s1-s. We parameterize the noise level by ξ:=1−s∈(0,1)\xi:=1-s\in(0,1), where larger ξ\xi means heavier noise.

DP traversal.

Fig. 2(a) shows the empirical DP curves obtained by sweeping the lookahead tt from ss (MMSE) to 11 (full perception) across four noise levels ξ∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7}\xi\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\}. As expected, the average denoiser traces smooth, monotone curves in the DP plane: increasing tt improves perception (lower FID) at the cost of distortion (higher RMSE). The resulting curves exhibit the convex shape predicted by the optimal DP function. Unlike prior methods that provide only discrete or heuristic control, our approach yields a smooth and continuous parameterization of the DP frontier from a single trained model.

We also observe that the traversal range increases with the noise level. For ξ=0.1\xi=0.1, the range is narrow since the MMSE estimator is already close to the data distribution, whereas for ξ=0.7\xi=0.7, the lookahead spans a wide range of operating points. This is consistent with Freirich et al. (2021), as the perception gap P∗P^{*} grows with noise, allowing a larger tradeoff between distortion and perception. Fig. 30 illustrates this effect: as tt increases from ss to 11, reconstructions transition from smooth averages to sharp, detailed images.

Variance restoration.

A natural question is why increasing the lookahead improves perceptual quality. A simple explanation follows from the law of total variance: for any noisy observation 𝐱s{\mathbf{x}}_{s}, we have Var⁡(𝐱1)=Var⁡(𝔼⁡[𝐱1∣𝐱s])+𝔼⁡[Var⁡(𝐱1∣𝐱s)]\mathrm{Var}({\mathbf{x}}_{1})=\mathrm{Var}\!\big(\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{s}]\big)+\mathbb{E}\!\big[\mathrm{Var}({\mathbf{x}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{s})\big]. Since the second term is strictly positive, the MMSE estimator Ds​(𝐱s)=𝔼⁡[𝐱1∣𝐱s]D_{s}({\mathbf{x}}_{s})=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{s}] has lower variance than the true data, i.e., Var⁡(Ds​(𝐱s))<Var⁡(𝐱1)\mathrm{Var}(D_{s}({\mathbf{x}}_{s}))<\mathrm{Var}({\mathbf{x}}_{1}). This variance gap leads to reduced contrast and over-smoothed reconstructions, and is precisely what the optimal DP estimator (9) corrects via interpolation. As the lookahead tt increases, the average denoiser progressively restores this variance, effectively traversing the same tradeoff within a single model. Fig. 2(b) supports this empirically: the relationship between variance ratio and FID is nearly identical across noise levels, suggesting that variance restoration underlies the observed perceptual improvements.

4 Plug-and-play with average denoisers

We now embed the average denoiser (10) into the PnP framework from Section 2.2 to solve general inverse problems with continuous DP control. Importantly, the DP interpretation applies at the level of the denoiser Ds,tD_{s,t}, while the overall PnP solution reflects its interaction with the forward model. As a result, in general inverse problems, the lookahead controls a tradeoff that combines perceptual alignment with data-consistency effects, rather than exactly reproducing the denoising DP frontier.

Algorithm.

Given a trained flow map 𝐯θ​(⋅,s,t){\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}(\cdot,s,t), observations 𝐲{\mathbf{y}}, and a chosen lookahead t∈[s,1]t\in[s,1], our method alternates between a gradient descent step on the data-fidelity term g⁡(𝐱)=12​‖𝐲−f⁡(𝐱)‖2g({\mathbf{x}})=\tfrac{1}{2}\|{\mathbf{y}}-f({\mathbf{x}})\|^{2} and a proximal step utilizing the average denoiser. Following (Martin et al., 2025), we include a renoising step prior to applying the denoiser. This reprojects the gradient-updated iterate onto the support of the distribution at noise level ss, ensuring that the average denoiser Ds,tD_{s,t} processes inputs at its intended operational noise level. The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1.

Role of the renoising step.

The stochastic renoising step is what makes the lookahead a DP knob in the inverse-problem setting. With renoising, Ds,tD_{s,t} operates at its intended noise level ss, placing it in the regime where Theorem 1 characterizes its behavior, and the injected noise restores the sample diversity required at the perceptual end of the frontier. Without renoising, the iteration reduces to a fixed-point Tikhonov estimator and the lookahead degenerates into a bias-variance knob; we treat this case in Appendix D.4.

Computational cost and connection to PnP-Flow.

Algorithm 1 requires one forward pass through 𝐯θ{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta} per iteration. The lookahead tt is merely a conditioning input, adding zero overhead and preserving efficiency over methods requiring ODE backpropagation or trace computations.

5 Related work

Consistency models and flow maps for inverse problems.

Consistency models (Song et al., 2023b) learn to map any point on a probability flow ODE to its origin, enabling single-step generation. Consistency trajectory models (Kim et al., 2025) and flow maps (Boffi et al., 2025a) generalize this to arbitrary pairs (s,t)(s,t) by learning the ODE solution operator. More recent works repurposed these models for controlled generation, either as guided samplers (Sabour et al., 2025a; Spagnoletti et al., 2025; Garber and Tirer, 2025; Holderrieth et al., 2026), as priors (Gülle et al., 2026), or for optimizing the noise initialization (Mammadov et al., 2026). Most recently, and concurrently to this work, Huang et al. (2026) also leverage flow maps for guidance, formulating reward-based generation as an optimal control problem and using the flow map for fast guided sampling. However, all these approaches primarily target accelerated sampling at a fixed operating point and do not provide explicit control over the restoration tradeoff. In contrast, we treat the lookahead tt as a continuous parameter, turning a single flow map into a family of estimators that spans the entire distortion–perception (DP) frontier.

Methods that traverse the DP plane.

Recent approaches explore distortion–perception control by learning data-dependent flows between degraded and clean distributions. Inversion by Direct Iteration (InDI) (Delbracio and Milanfar, 2023) and stochastic interpolants (Albergo et al., 2024) learn flows from measurements to clean images, while Posterior-Mean Rectified Flow (PMRF) (Ohayon et al., 2025) replaces the source distribution with an approximation of the posterior mean. These methods provide inference-time mechanisms for traversing the DP plane, either through integration schedules or through a scalar parameter that controls the interpolation between posterior-mean and perceptual reconstructions. However, they rely on supervised training with paired dat (𝐲,𝐱)({\mathbf{y}},{\mathbf{x}}) and, in the case of PMRF, require an auxiliary model to estimate the posterior mean. Moreover, extending such approaches to handle different degradations generally requires collecting paired training data across those operators and scaling model capacity accordingly. In contrast, our approach learns a single unconditional flow map from clean images alone, whose lookahead parameter naturally induces a continuous family of denoisers. As a result, DP control is obtained from a single model without paired supervision, auxiliary networks, or retraining, and extends naturally to arbitrary forward operators through Plug-and-Play inference.

6 Numerical experiments

We now focus on the numerical results. Throughout the experiments, we aim to (i)(i) demonstrate competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods, and (i​i)(ii) show that our method uniquely enables continuous traversal of the DP plane with a single model.

Setup.

We evaluate all methods in two datasets: Celeba 128×128128\times 128 and AFHQ 256×256256\times 256; we also consider AFHQ-cats 192×192192\times 192. For each dataset, we train a flow map model vθ​(𝐱,s,t)v_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}},s,t), parametrized by the Song UNet architecture (Song et al., 2020; Ronneberger et al., 2015), from scratch using the off-diagonal loss of LSD described in (5). More training details can be found in Appendix B.1. We assess the reconstruction quality of the different samplers with mean squared error (in terms of PSNR=−10​log10​MSE\mathrm{PSNR}=-10\log_{10}\mathrm{MSE}) and two perceptual metrics, LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) and DISTS (Ding et al., 2020). In addition, we compute the FID Heusel et al. (2017) and KID Bińkowski et al. (2018) between ensembles of test set images and posterior samples. We compute the average of 100 samples, and for all the methods we consider Gaussian noise with σ=0.05\sigma=0.05, unless random inpainting with σ=0.01\sigma=0.01; also, in Appendix C.2.2 we include an experiment with Poisson noise.

We compared with recent methods that leverage pre-trained flow models, namely OT-ODE (Pokle et al., 2024), Flow Priors (Zhang et al., 2024), D-Flow (Ben-Hamu et al., 2024), DPS-ODE (Chung et al., 2023) and PnP-Flow (Martin et al., 2025), which corresponds to our proposed method for t=st=s. For all the models, we performed a search grid of hyperparameters to obtain the best performance possible, and we use the same trained network for the prior/regularizer; we defer to Appendix B.2 for further details. We also include a comparison with baselines using a flow matching model as prior (a model trained without the second loss in (5)), which can be found in App. C.4.

6.1 Inverse problems

We evaluate on the following tasks: (i)(i) motion deblurring with random kernel genearted with the code11 1 https://github.com/LeviBorodenko/motionblur and size 31×3131\times 31 (CelebA) and 61×6161\times 61 (AFHQ) and σb=1\sigma_{b}=1; (i​i)(ii) random inpainting with 90%90\% missing pixels; (i​i​i)(iii) super-resolution (×4\times 4); and (i​v)(iv) Gaussian deblurring, which are deferred to Appendix C.2.

Quantitative results are reported in Table 1 (with error bars in Appendix C.1), and visual results in Appendix C.5 and Fig. 5. PnP-Flow with t=st=s achieves the best or near-best PSNR across all four (dataset, task) settings, confirming that the average denoiser at small lookaheads behaves as a low-distortion estimator. At the other extreme, PnP-Flow with t=1t=1 achieves the best or near-best LPIPS DISTS and FID on every task; on inpainting, it matches DPS-ODE on FID while substantially improving LPIPS and DISTS. Competing methods either commit to a single operating point (DPS-ODE favors perception, D-Flow favors distortion) or fall short on both, whereas our approach attains both regimes from a single trained network. Beyond accuracy, PnP-Flow is also the fastest of the methods compared, as shown in Appendix B.3. Lastly, we note that PnP-Flow with t=1t=1 is not uniformly the best perceptual method in all tasks. In particular, on Gaussian deblurring and super-resolution (in Appendix C.2), some baselines achieve better perceptual metrics. Nevertheless, increasing the lookahead from t=st=s to t=1t=1 consistently shifts PnP-Flow toward the perceptual end of the DP spectrum, substantially improving FID, LPIPS, and DISTS relative to the distortion-oriented regime. We therefore view the main contribution not as identifying a universally optimal perceptual operating point, but as providing a principled mechanism for continuously traversing the DP tradeoff with a single trained model (see Appendix C.8 for further discussion).

6.2 Analysis of the DP tradeoff

We now analyze how the lookahead parameter tt controls the characteristics of our reconstructions by moving in DP plane. We evaluate the average denoiser {Ds,t}t\{D_{s,t}\}_{t} at multiple lookahead values within a PnP solver and report RMSE (distortion) against FID (perception); for box inpainting, we use a mask of size 80×8080\times 80.

Results are in in Fig. 3, and three observations stand out. First, varying tt produces a smooth, (almost) monotonic trajectory in the DP plane: small lookaheads yields minimum RMSE, large lookaheads minimum FID, and intermediate values smoothly interpolate between the two. This empirically confirms our analysis from Section 3.2.1 and shows that the behavior extends to natural images and general degradations. Second, the same qualitative trend appears across all five inverse problems — Gaussian deblurring, motion deblurring, random/box inpainting, and super-resolution — despite the very different forward operators, suggesting that the DP control given by tt is degradation-agnostic. Third, no single tt is universally best: the optimal lookahead depends on the user’s preference between distortion and perception, which is precisely the use case our framework is designed to support.

Non-linear inverse problems.

Finally, we evaluate the DP tradeoff on JPEG compression, a non-linear degradation, with quantization factor 10. We study the effect of the number of PnP iterations; the results are shown in Fig. 4 for AFHQ; see Appendix C.2.1 for comparison with baselines. PnP with flow maps consistently achieves better perceptual quality. However, increasing the number of iterations eventually degrades FID, consistent with observations in other inverse problems.

7 Discussion and limitations

We introduced flow map denoisers, a generalization of the standard instantaneous denoiser that enables continuous, zero-shot traversal of the DP tradeoff. By reinterpreting flow maps as a continuum of average denoisers indexed by a lookahead parameter tt, we link flow maps to the theory of optimal DP estimators. This traversal is provably optimal for Gaussian targets and empirically validated for natural images. Embedded within a Plug-and-Play (PnP) solver, our approach enables inference-time control over restoration quality across diverse degradations, without retraining, paired data, or auxiliary models.

Our approach has several limitations. First, the formal optimality result is restricted to the Gaussian case. While the image experiments in Section 3.3 suggest similar behavior more broadly, a general theoretical characterization remains open. In particular, understanding failure modes is an important direction for future work, as certain degradations can lead to non-monotonic DP behavior, like box inpainting in Fig 3. Second, flow map models are more expensive to train than standard flow matching models and may underperform on pure distortion metrics such as PSNR. Third, while increasing the lookahead parameter consistently moves reconstructions toward the perceptual end of the DP spectrum, the resulting endpoint (t=1t=1) is not always the best perceptual method. This suggests that the lookahead parameter should primarily be viewed as a mechanism for traversing the DP tradeoff rather than as a way of reaching the optimal perceptual operating point for every restoration task.

The perspective in this work opens several directions for future work, borrowing ideas from the denoiser literature (Milanfar and Delbracio, 2025). Average denoisers could be trained directly via denoising objectives, such as SURE-based/consistency losses (Raphan and Simoncelli, 2011; Daras et al., 2025; Tachella et al., 2025). Extending the construction to more general noising processes, such as general restoration priors (Hu et al., 2024; Elata et al., 2025), is an additional natural next step. Lastly, our experiments are limited to pixel-space models (CelebA 128, AFHQ 256); extending the framework to latent-space and text-to-image settings is an important direction.

Appendix

Appendix A Background

A.1 Flow Maps

Consider a probability flow defined by the ordinary differential equation

𝐱˙t=𝐯t​(𝐱t),𝐱0∼p0,\dot{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t}={\mathbf{v}}_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{t}),\quad{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim p_{0},

which transports samples from a simple distribution p0p_{0} to a target distribution p1p_{1}. The associated flow map 𝐗s,t:ℝd→ℝd{\mathbf{X}}_{s,t}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is defined as the solution operator of this ODE:

Xs,t​(𝐱s)=𝐱t,X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}}_{s})={\mathbf{x}}_{t},

i.e., it maps a point at time ss to its position at time tt along the flow trajectory. In particular, X0,1X_{0,1} directly maps samples from p0p_{0} to p1p_{1}, enabling one-step generation without numerical integration. A convenient parameterization of the flow map is given by

Xs,t​(𝐱)=𝐱+(t−s)​𝐯​(𝐱,s,t),X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{x}}+(t-s)\,{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},s,t),

where 𝐯s,t{\mathbf{v}}_{s,t} can be interpreted as the average velocity between times ss and tt. In the limit t→st\to s, this recovers the instantaneous velocity field:

lims→t∂tXs,t​(𝐱)=𝐯⁡(𝐱,t),\lim_{s\to t}\partial_{t}X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t),

which implies that 𝐯⁡(𝐱,t,t)=𝐯⁡(𝐱,t){\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t,t)={\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t).

Characterization of the flow map.

The flow map can be equivalently characterized in three ways:

  • •

    Lagrangian form:

    ∂tXs,t​(𝐱)=𝐯t​(Xs,t​(𝐱)),\partial_{t}X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{v}}_{t}(X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})),

    which describes evolution along trajectories;

  • •

    Eulerian form:

    ∂sXs,t​(𝐱)+∇Xs,t​(𝐱)​𝐯s​(𝐱)=0,\partial_{s}X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})+\nabla X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})\,{\mathbf{v}}_{s}({\mathbf{x}})=0,

    which expresses conservation along the flow;

  • •

    Semigroup property:

    Xs,t​(𝐱)=Xu,t​(Xs,u​(𝐱)),X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})=X_{u,t}(X_{s,u}({\mathbf{x}})),

    which encodes consistency across time intervals.

These equivalent formulations provide the basis for learning flow maps in practice (Boffi et al., 2025b).

Self-distillation framework.

Instead of learning the instantaneous velocity field 𝐯(.,t){\mathbf{v}}(.,t) and integrating the ODE, flow map models directly learn 𝐯(.,s,t){\mathbf{v}}(.,s,t) by combining:

  • •

    the diagonal loss in (2) enforcing 𝐯⁡(𝐱,t,t)≈𝐯⁡(𝐱,t){\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t,t)\approx{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t),

  • •

    an off-diagonal loss enforcing consistency with one of the above three characterizations.

Notice that throughout this work we used the LSD loss in (5), which is the one associated to the Lagrangian condition. This approach, known as self-distillation, allows training a single model that approximates the full flow map Xs,tX_{s,t} without requiring a pre-trained teacher model.

A.2 Inverse problems with flow/diffusion priors

While in this work we focus on flow-based models, there is a large body of works using diffusion priors, which are very related to our proposed method. We now summarize some of this early works.

These methods generate a sample from the posterior by running the reverse process using conditional score at tt obtained via Bayes’ rule as

∇𝐱t​log​p​(𝐱t|𝐲)=∇𝐱t​log​p​(𝐲|𝐱t)+∇𝐱t​log​p​(𝐱t).\nabla_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}\log p({\mathbf{x}}_{t}|{\mathbf{y}})=\nabla_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}\log p({\mathbf{y}}|{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+\nabla_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}\log p({\mathbf{x}}_{t}). (14)

While the second term uses a pre-trained diffusion model, the first is intractable, as seen from p⁡(𝐲|𝐱t)=∫p⁡(𝐲|𝐱0)​p​(𝐱0|𝐱t)​d​𝐱0p({\mathbf{y}}|{\mathbf{x}}_{t})=\int p({\mathbf{y}}|{\mathbf{x}}_{0})p({\mathbf{x}}_{0}|{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\text{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{0}. Prior works (Chung et al., 2023; Song et al., 2022; Kadkhodaie and Simoncelli, 2021; Song et al., 2023a) address this with a Gaussian approximation of p⁡(𝐱0|𝐱t)p({\mathbf{x}}_{0}|{\mathbf{x}}_{t}) using Tweedie’s formula 𝔼⁡[𝐱0|𝐱t]=1αt​(𝐱t−σt​ϵ𝜽​(𝐱t,t))\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{0}|{\mathbf{x}}_{t}]=\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\left({\mathbf{x}}_{t}-\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)\right). Still, this requires the computation of the score Jacobian, which is computationally expensive, especially for pixel-based models at high-resolution. In fact, this approximation is the one used for DPS-ODE in Section 6.

Beyond guidance and PnP/optimization-based techniques, there is a body of works using sequential monte carlo (SMC) (Wu et al., 2023). In a nutshell, these methods leverage particle-based techniques, which allows to target the exact posterior in the particle limit.

Appendix B Implementation

B.1 Training details

All models are trained unconditionally using the Flow Map objective (Boffi et al., 2025b) with the LSD loss (5).

Architecture.

We use the SongUNet Song et al. (2021) – a UNet with self-attention – with a base channel width of 128 and channel multipliers [1,2,3,4][1,2,3,4], giving four resolution scales. Self-attention is applied at spatial resolutions 16×1616\times 16 and 8×88\times 8. Each resolution level contains 3 residual blocks, dropout rate 0.10.1, and a cosine resampling filter [1,3,3,1][1,3,3,1].

Time conditioning.

The network is conditioned on two scalars (αr,αt)∈[0,1]2(\alpha_{r},\alpha_{t})\in[0,1]^{2} representing the interpolation times of the source and target. Both are encoded with a positional (sinusoidal) embedding. Following Boffi et al. (2025b), the two conditioning scalars are embedded as PE⁡(αt−αr)\mathrm{PE}(\alpha_{t}-\alpha_{r}) and PE⁡(αr)\mathrm{PE}(\alpha_{r}), summed, and passed through a two-layer MLP with SiLU activations to produce a global conditioning vector injected into every residual block via adaptive group normalisation.

Loss weighting.

For the off-diagonal term, we sample s,ts,t uniformly from {(s,t):0<s<t≤1}\{(s,t):0<s<t\leq 1\} as detailed in Boffi et al. (2025b). We follow Karras et al. (2024) and learn a per-sample uncertainty weight for the LSD loss, we attach a small network that outputs a scalar log-variance log⁡σ2​(αr,αt)∈ℝ\log\sigma^{2}(\alpha_{r},\alpha_{t})\in\mathbb{R} per training example. The network takes the concatenated pair [αr,αt]∈ℝB×2×H×W[\alpha_{r},\alpha_{t}]\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 2\times H\times W} and generate a scalar used to weight the loss as ℒ∝e−log⁡σ2​ℓ+log⁡σ2\mathcal{L}\propto e^{-\log\sigma^{2}}\,\ell+\log\sigma^{2}.

Datasets and resolution.
  • •

    CelebA-HQ ×128128\!\times\!128 Liu et al. (2015): 202,599 images; 90% train split.

  • •

    AFHQ ×256256\!\times\!256 Choi et al. (2020): 16,130 images; 90% train split.

During training, 75% of the batch is used for the on-diagonal loss, while the remaining 25% for the off-diagonal one. Augmentation (horizontal flip, rotation, scaling, anisotropic scaling, translation) is applied with probability p=0.12p=0.12.

Optimization.

All models are optimized with Adam (Kingma, 2015) (β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, ε=10−8\varepsilon=10^{-8}) at a learning rate of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} with no learning-rate schedule.

Compute.

For training, we use 8 NVIDIA GPUs A100, while for inference we use a single GPU for all methods.

B.2 Hyperparameters and baselines

For all baselines, unless otherwise specified, we use σ=0.05\sigma=0.05 for Gaussian/motion deblurring and super-resolution, and σ=0.01\sigma=0.01 for inpainting. Blur kernel size is set to 61 for AFHQ and 31 for CelebA.

Flow-Priors (Zhang et al., 2024).

We follow the original parameterization with guidance weight λ\lambda and step size η\eta. We use λ=105\lambda=10^{5}, η=10−2\eta=10^{-2}, and K=1K=1 inner iteration in all settings. The number of outer iterations is fixed to N=100N=100.

D-Flow (Ben-Hamu et al., 2024).

We tune the regularization parameter λ∈{0.1,0.01,0.001}\lambda\in\{0.1,0.01,0.001\} and the initialization blending parameter α∈{0.1,0.3,0.5}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5\}, retaining λ=0.01\lambda=0.01 and α=0.1\alpha=0.1. As recommended by the authors, the inner LBFGS optimization runs for 2020 iterations and the ODE is solved with 66 Euler steps. The number of outer iterations is fixed to 2020.

OT-ODE (Pokle et al., 2024).

We tune the initial time t0∈{0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4}t_{0}\in\{0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\} and the step-size schedule γ∈{constant,t}\gamma\in\{\text{constant},\sqrt{t}\}. We use γ=constant\gamma=\text{constant} throughout. The retained values are t0=0.1t_{0}=0.1 for inpainting, t0=0.3t_{0}=0.3 for Gaussian deblurring and super-resolution, and t0=0.4t_{0}=0.4 for motion deblurring on AFHQ. The number of iterations is fixed to N=100N=100.

DPS-ODE (Chung et al., 2023).

This methods corresponds to the ODE (deterministic) version of the original DPS designed for diffusion models. We tune the guidance weight η∈{102,103,104}\eta\in\{10^{2},10^{3},10^{4}\}, retaining η=103\eta=10^{3} as default, η=102\eta=10^{2} on CelebA box inpainting, and η=102\eta=10^{2} on AFHQ Gaussian deblurring. The number of iterations is fixed to N=100N=100.

PnP-Flow w/ t=st=s (Martin et al., 2025) and w/ t=1t=1 (ours).

We adjust the learning-rate exponent α∈{0.05,0.1}\alpha\in\{0.05,0.1\} and the number of time steps N∈{30,50,100,300}N\in\{30,50,100,300\}. We use α=0.05\alpha=0.05 in most settings and α=0.1\alpha=0.1 for motion deblurring; N=100N=100 by default, N=300N=300 for hard random inpainting on AFHQ, and N∈{30,50}N\in\{30,50\} for motion deblurring.

B.3 Computational cost

Running time.

Table 3 reports per-image reconstruction times on a single A100 GPU. PnP-Flow is the fastest method we compare against, while reaching perceptual quality typically associated with posterior sampling. This illustrates a concrete advantage of using a flow map as a PnP denoiser: it inherits the speed of MAP-style approaches without sacrificing perceptual fidelity.

Memory footprint.

Overall, almost all the methods fit in a single A100 with a batch of 5 images for AFHQ 256x256; the only one that could not fit is D-flow, which needed to use a single image per batch.

B.4 Experiment of the teaser plot

We detail here the experiment underlying Fig. 1. The data distribution p1p_{1} is a 2D isotropic mixture of Gaussians,

p1=12​𝒩​(𝝁a,σc2​𝐈)+12​𝒩​(𝝁b,σc2​𝐈),𝝁a=(4.5,3.5),𝝁b=(3.5,5.5),σc=0.35.p_{1}=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a},\sigma_{c}^{2}{\mathbf{I}})+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b},\sigma_{c}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}),\quad\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a}=(4.5,3.5),\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_{b}=(3.5,5.5),\ \sigma_{c}=0.35.

Observations are generated according to the linear forward model in (6), with f⁡(⋅)=𝐇f(\cdot)={\mathbf{H}} a fixed rotation of angle π/6\pi/6 followed by isotropic rescaling.

Similarly to the case in Appendix D.3, the MMSE denoiser Ds​(x)=𝔼⁡[X1∣Xs=x]D_{s}(x)=\mathbb{E}[X_{1}\mid X_{s}=x] admits a closed-form expression via the component posteriors. We use this analytic denoiser to construct the flow-map denoiser

Ds,t​(𝐱)=𝐱+(1−s)​𝐯​(𝐱,s,t),𝐯⁡(𝐱,s,t),=1t−s​∫stDτ​(𝐱τ)−𝐱τ1−τ​𝑑τ,D_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{x}}+(1-s)\,{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},s,t),\quad{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},s,t),=\frac{1}{t-s}\int_{s}^{t}\frac{D_{\tau}({\mathbf{x}}_{\tau})-{\mathbf{x}}_{\tau}}{1-\tau}\,d\tau,

where the average velocity is approximated by Euler integration of the flow 𝐱˙τ=(Dτ​(𝐱τ)−𝐱τ)/(1−τ)\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{\tau}=(D_{\tau}({\mathbf{x}}_{\tau})-{\mathbf{x}}_{\tau})/(1-\tau) using 100100 steps. Using this approximation of the average denoiser, we run PnP-Flow in Alg. 1 with s=0.45s=0.45 (which is fixed to isolate the behavior of the lookahead), step size γk=λ​1−k/K\gamma_{k}=\lambda\sqrt{1-k/K} with λ=0.4\lambda=0.4, and K=50K=50 iterations. We initialize with 𝐱(0)=𝐇−1​𝐲{\mathbf{x}}^{(0)}={\mathbf{H}}^{-1}{\mathbf{y}} and run the algorithm independently for each sample. We consider three lookaheads t∈{s,s+0.27, 1}t\in\{s,\,s+0.27,\,1\}, corresponding to the MMSE, an intermediate, and the full lookahead regime.

The behavior follows the distortion–perception tradeoff: at t=st=s, reconstructions collapse toward the inter-mode mean (low variance, high distortion), while at t=1t=1 the bimodal structure is recovered (higher perceptual quality). Intermediate lookaheads interpolate smoothly between these regimes, all using a single denoiser.

C.1 Results with error bars

C.2 Additional inverse problems

Gaussian deblurring.

We consider a box of size 80×8080\times 80 for AFHQ and 60×6060\times 60 for CelebA. The quantitative results are in Table 8.

C.2.1 Non-linear

JPEG.

We consider JPEG, following the setting from Section 6.2. Given that OT-ODE and Flow priors cannot handle non-linear degradations, we only compare with DPS-ODE; the result is shown in Table 9 for AFHQ.

Colorization.

We consider also Colorization; the result is shown in Table 10 for AFHQ.

C.2.2 Gaussian deblurring with Poisson noise

Lastly, we consider Poisson noise, showing that our analysis goes beyond Gaussian noise. In particular, we normalized each image to [0,1][0,1], and consider an independent Poisson process normalised by a peak rate λ>0\lambda>0:

yi|𝐱∼Poisson(λ(𝐇𝐱)i),i=1,…,N,y_{i}\,\big|\,{\mathbf{x}}\;\sim\;\mathrm{Poisson}\!\big(\lambda\,({\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}})_{i}\big),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N, (15)

so that 𝔼⁡[yi∣𝐱]=(𝐇𝐱)i\mathbb{E}[y_{i}\mid{\mathbf{x}}]=({\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}})_{i} and Var⁡[yi∣𝐱]=(𝐇𝐱)i/λ\mathrm{Var}[y_{i}\mid{\mathbf{x}}]=({\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}})_{i}/\lambda. The signal-to-noise ratio scales as λ\sqrt{\lambda}, where lower λ\lambda corresponds to fewer photons and a noisier observation; we consider λ=20\lambda=20. Given this noise model, the corresponding negative log-likelihood, used as the data-fidelity term in Alg. 1, is (up to a constant in 𝐱{\mathbf{x}})

g⁡(𝐱)=∑i=1N[(𝐇𝐱)i−yi​log⁡(𝐇𝐱)i].g({\mathbf{x}})\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big[\,({\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}})_{i}\,-\,y_{i}\log({\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}})_{i}\,\big]. (16)

The results as a function of the number of steps is shown in Fig. 6, while qualitative comparisons are in Fig. 17.

C.3 Distortion-perception of CelebA

We include here the same plot as in Section 2.3; it is shown in Fig. 7. Again, varying tt produces a smooth, monotonic trajectory in the DP plane: small lookaheads minimize RMSE, large lookaheads minimize FID, and intermediate values smoothly interpolate between the two.

C.4 Comparison with baselines using a flow matching model

Table 11 compares all methods under both a flow matching backbone and a flow map backbone, allowing us to isolate the contribution of the flow map training objective from the choice of sampler.

Flow matching backbone.

PnP-Flow (t=st=s) achieves the highest PSNR (25.3625.36 dB), but at the cost of perceptual quality relative to Flow-priors (LPIPS 0.3590.359 vs. 0.2050.205). PnP-Flow (t=1t=1) is inapplicable here, as it requires the consistency property enforced only by flow map training.

Impact of the backbone.

The results are largely consistent across backbones, with DPS-ODE achieving a lower FID with the flow matching model. However, the flow map backbone with PnP-flow (t=1t=1) still yields notably lower FID scores throughout and is required to unlock PnP-flow (t=1t=1).

C.5 Visual results

C.6 Visualization of the iterations for different lookaheads

C.7 Performance as a function of the number of PnP iterations

We study how the two endpoint lookaheads, t=st=s and t=1t=1, depend on the number of PnP iterations NN. Results for AFHQ are reported on super-resolution ×4\times 4 (Fig. 24), Gaussian deblurring (Fig. 25) and box inpainting (Fig. 26); we also include for CelebA in Fig. 27.

The two regimes behave qualitatively differently. At t=st=s, both RMSE and FID decrease monotonically with NN and plateau, consistent with the local-contraction analysis of Theorem 2. At t=1t=1, the perceptual trajectory is non-monotonic: FID drops sharply within the first few tens of iterations, reaches its minimum, and then drifts back up as NN continues to grow. The effect is most pronounced for Gaussian deblurring, where the best FID at t=1t=1 (≈11\approx 11 at N≈20N\approx 20) is reached an order of magnitude earlier than the best FID at t=st=s (≈23.5\approx 23.5 at N≈300N\approx 300). This behavior is consistent with the lookahead-dependent contraction factor in Theorem 2. The local Lipschitz constant LDloc​(t)L_{D}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t) grows with tt, reflecting the transition from a contractive MMSE estimator at t=st=s to a less regular, perceptually-oriented estimator at t=1t=1. RMSE remains well-behaved in both cases, indicating that the drift is along the perceptual axis.

The practical takeaway is that the two endpoints call for different iteration schemes: the perceptual endpoint (t=1t=1) is best run for fewer steps than the distortion endpoint (t=st=s). The values of NN used in our main experiments (Appendix B.2) reflect this asymmetry. This behavior also explains why flow maps and consistency models are useful denoisers for solving restoration problem with few-steps as in (Spagnoletti et al., 2025; Gülle et al., 2026).

C.8 Failure modes and limitations

While our contributions is using flow maps as denoisers in a PnP scheme, enhancing the perceptual quality of the estimated image, we observed that for some degradations, the DP traversing might not hold exactly. For instance, in phase retrieval with oversample of 4, we observe that PnP with flow maps outperform the instantaneous denoiser case (t=st=s) only after certain number of steps, as shown in Fig. 28. Furthermore, the overall performance is not strong, as shown quantiative in Table 12 and qualitative in Fig. 29.

D.3 Experiment on Mixture-of-Gaussians

D.3.1 MMSE denoiser for a mixture of Gaussians

Setup.

Let p0=𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)p_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) and p1=12​𝒩​(𝝁a,σc2​𝐈)+12​𝒩​(𝝁b,σc2​𝐈)p_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a},\sigma_{c}^{2}\mathbf{I})+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b},\sigma_{c}^{2}\mathbf{I}). Under the linear interpolant 𝐱t=(1−t)​𝐱0+t​𝐱1{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=(1-t){\mathbf{x}}_{0}+t{\mathbf{x}}_{1}, we seek to compute the MMSE denoiser:

Dt​(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[𝐱1∣𝐱t=𝐱].D_{t}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{t}={\mathbf{x}}]. (30)
Step 1: Marginal distribution of 𝐱t{\mathbf{x}}_{t}.

Conditioned on 𝐱1{\mathbf{x}}_{1} originating from component k∈{a,b}k\in\{a,b\}, we have 𝐱1∼𝒩⁡(𝝁k,σc2​𝐈){\mathbf{x}}_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k},\sigma_{c}^{2}\mathbf{I}) and 𝐱0∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈){\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}). Thus:

𝐱t∣component k∼𝒩(t𝝁k,σt2𝐈),where σt2=(1−t)2+t2σc2.{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\mid\text{component }k\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}\!\left(t\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k},\;\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right),\quad\text{where }\sigma_{t}^{2}=(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma_{c}^{2}. (31)

The marginal distribution is the mixture:

p⁡(𝐱t)=12​𝒩​(𝐱t,t​𝝁a,σt2​𝐈)+12​𝒩​(𝐱t,t​𝝁b,σt2​𝐈).p({\mathbf{x}}_{t})=\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{x}}_{t};\,t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a},\,\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I})+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{x}}_{t};\,t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b},\,\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}). (32)
Step 2: Posterior weights.

By Bayes’ rule, the posterior probability wk​(𝐱,t)w_{k}({\mathbf{x}},t) that 𝐱1{\mathbf{x}}_{1} originated from component kk given 𝐱t=𝐱{\mathbf{x}}_{t}={\mathbf{x}} is:

wk​(𝐱,t)=𝒩⁡(𝐱,t​𝝁k,σt2​𝐈)𝒩⁡(𝐱,t​𝝁a,σt2​𝐈)+𝒩⁡(𝐱,t​𝝁b,σt2​𝐈).w_{k}({\mathbf{x}},t)=\frac{\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{x}};\,t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k},\,\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I})}{\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{x}};\,t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a},\,\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I})+\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{x}};\,t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b},\,\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I})}. (33)

In log-space, this is proportional to −‖𝐱−t​𝝁k‖22​σt2-\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}-t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\|^{2}}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}}, and the weights are normalized via softmax such that wa+wb=1w_{a}+w_{b}=1.

Step 3: Conditional mean within components.

Given that 𝐱1{\mathbf{x}}_{1} comes from component kk, the posterior mean of 𝐱1{\mathbf{x}}_{1} given 𝐱t=𝐱{\mathbf{x}}_{t}={\mathbf{x}} is:

𝔼[𝐱1∣𝐱t=𝐱,component k]=𝝁k+At(𝐱−t𝝁k),\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{t}={\mathbf{x}},\text{component }k]=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}+A_{t}({\mathbf{x}}-t\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}), (34)

where At=t​σc2σt2A_{t}=\frac{t\,\sigma_{c}^{2}}{\sigma_{t}^{2}} is the regression coefficient (Tweedie’s formula applied component-wise).

Step 4: Full MMSE denoiser.

By the law of total expectation, the denoiser is the weighted average:

Dt​(𝐱)=wa​(𝐱,t)​[𝝁a+At​(𝐱−t​𝝁a)]+wb​(𝐱,t)​[𝝁b+At​(𝐱−t​𝝁b)].D_{t}({\mathbf{x}})=w_{a}({\mathbf{x}},t)\,\left[\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a}+A_{t}({\mathbf{x}}-t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a})\right]+w_{b}({\mathbf{x}},t)\,\left[\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b}+A_{t}({\mathbf{x}}-t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b})\right]. (35)

This is a softmax-weighted average of the within-component posterior means. Its behavior is intuitive:

  • •

    When 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} is close to t​𝝁at\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a}, wa≈1w_{a}\approx 1 and Dt​(𝐱)≈𝝁a+At​(𝐱−t​𝝁a)D_{t}({\mathbf{x}})\approx\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a}+A_{t}({\mathbf{x}}-t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a}) (assigned to component aa).

  • •

    When 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} is equidistant from t​𝝁at\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a} and t​𝝁bt\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b}, wa≈wb≈0.5w_{a}\approx w_{b}\approx 0.5, and Dt​(𝐱)D_{t}({\mathbf{x}}) averages the two, producing an output between the modes (the posterior averaging artifact).

We compute the average denoiser by ODE integration using the instantaneous velocity field. The nonlinearity introduced by the softmax weights makes the MoG fundamentally different from the single Gaussian case: the denoiser is non-linear in 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}, the flow map lacks a closed-form solution, and the posterior averaging artifact (blurring between modes) emerges as a direct consequence of the mixture structure. However, given the simplicity of the instantaneous denoiser, we can approximate the average denoiser numerically.

D.3.2 DP analysis

In this section, we consider a controlled setting based on a 2D mixture of Gaussians. For this distsribution, the marginal velocity admits a closed-form expression, allowing both the average denoiser Ds,tD_{s,t} and the optimal DP estimator of Freirich et al. (2021) to be evaluated with high precision, bypassing the requirement of a learned model.

Setup.

We consider 𝝁a=(−2,0)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a}=(-2,0), 𝝁b=(2,0)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b}=(2,0), and σc=0.3\sigma_{c}=0.3, and compute the average denoiser Ds,tD_{s,t} by integrating x˙τ=v⁡(xτ,τ)\dot{x}_{\tau}=v(x_{\tau},\tau) from τ=s\tau=s to τ=t\tau=t with a fourth-order Runge–Kutta scheme (200 steps).

Optimal DP construction.

To construct the optimal DP curve, we follow Freirich et al. (2021, Theorem 3). At perception level P∈[0,P∗]P\in[0,P^{*}], the optimal estimator is given by (9).

We approximate this construction empirically by drawing N=5000N=5000 samples, computing 𝐱^0(i)=Ds​(𝐱s(i))\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{(i)}=D_{s}({\mathbf{x}}_{s}^{(i)}), and solving the discrete optimal transport problem between the empirical distributions {𝐱^0(i)}\{\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{(i)}\} and {𝐱1(j)}∼p1\{{\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{(j)}\}\sim p_{1} using (Flamary et al., 2021). Let π\pi denote the optimal coupling; we then form the interpolated samples as

𝐱^P(i)=(1−PP∗)​𝐱^0(i)+PP∗​𝐱1(π⁡(i)).\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{P}^{(i)}=\left(1-\frac{P}{P^{*}}\right)\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{(i)}+\frac{P}{P^{*}}{\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{(\pi(i))}.

Distortion is measured as MSE with respect to the ground truth, while perception is quantified via the squared 2-Wasserstein distance W22​(p^,p1)W_{2}^{2}(\hat{p},p_{1}) between empirical distributions.

Results.

Fig. 31 compares the resulting curves at three noise levels s∈0.3,0.5,0.7s\in{0.3,0.5,0.7}, corresponding to heavy, moderate, and light noise (recall that smaller ss implies heavier noise, with ξ:=1−s\xi:=1-s). Three observations stand out.

  1. 1.

    Endpoints coincide at MMSE. At t=st=s (equivalently, α=1\alpha=1), both curves reduce to the MMSE estimator by construction, yielding identical distortion–perception coordinates across all panels.

  2. 2.

    Near-optimal behavior in the interior. For intermediate lookaheads, the average denoiser traces a DP curve that lies slightly above the Freirich optimum, with a small and nearly uniform gap. At s=0.3s=0.3 (heavy noise), this gap remains below 0.020.02 in MSE across the full perception range. This discrepancy is not a numerical artifact: it persists when using higher-order integration (RK4) and when increasing the sample size from N=2000N=2000 to N=5000N=5000. Instead, it reflects a structural limitation—while the flow-map trajectory matches the W2W_{2} geodesic in the Gaussian case, it deviates slightly for nonlinear velocity fields (here induced by the softmax-weighted mixture).

  3. 3.

    Endpoint behavior at t=1t=1. At the perceptual endpoint, the distribution Ds,1​(pxs)D_{s,1}(p_{x_{s}}) closely approximates p1p_{1} but does not match it exactly, resulting in a small residual W22W_{2}^{2} gap. This gap decreases as noise increases (from 9.4×10−39.4\times 10^{-3} at s=0.5s=0.5 to 3.8×10−33.8\times 10^{-3} at s=0.3s=0.3, compared to a sampling floor of 2.2×10−32.2\times 10^{-3}). This is consistent with the intuition that the integrable 1/(1−τ)1/(1-\tau) singularity in the velocity field has a stronger effect when the final integration interval is short.

Taken together, these results show that the average denoiser is near-optimal in a controlled setting: the resulting curves are smooth, monotone, and convex, match the MMSE endpoint exactly, and exhibit only small, well-characterized deviations from the Freirich optimum. This complements the exact optimality established in the Gaussian case (Theorem 1) and supports the behavior observed at image scale (Fig. 2(a)).

D.4 Fixed point characterization

We characterize the fixed-point solution of the PnP iteration and show its dependence on the lookahead tt. For simplicity, we consider linear inverse problems f⁡(𝐱)=𝐇𝐱f({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}} and analyze the deterministic variant of Algorithm 1 (i.e., ϵ=0\epsilon=0). In this variant, the stochastic renoising step reduces to the deterministic map Rs​(𝐳)=s​𝐳R_{s}({\mathbf{z}})=s\,{\mathbf{z}}, and the per-iteration operator becomes

Tt(𝐱):=Ds,t(Rs(Fλ(𝐱))),withFλ(𝐱)=𝐱−λ∇g(𝐱),Rs(𝐳)=s𝐳.T_{t}({\mathbf{x}}):=D_{s,t}\bigl(R_{s}(F_{\lambda}({\mathbf{x}}))\bigr),\quad\text{with}\quad F_{\lambda}({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{x}}-\lambda\nabla g({\mathbf{x}}),\quad R_{s}({\mathbf{z}})=s\,{\mathbf{z}}. (36)

Let LD​(t)L_{D}(t) denote the Lipschitz constant of Ds,tD_{s,t} and LF=‖𝐈−λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇‖L_{F}=\|{\mathbf{I}}-\lambda\,{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}\| that of FλF_{\lambda}. Global convergence would require TtT_{t} to be a contraction, i.e., s​LD​(t)​LF<1s\,L_{D}(t)\,L_{F}<1. The gradient step satisfies LF≤1L_{F}\leq 1 for any λ∈(0, 2/‖𝐇⊤​𝐇‖]\lambda\in(0,\,2/\|{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}\|], with equality (i.e., LF=1L_{F}=1) when 𝐇⊤​𝐇{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}} has zero eigenvalues, as in inpainting. In such ill-posed cases, contraction must come entirely from the composition s​LD​(t)s\,L_{D}(t). Empirically, however, s​LD​(t)​LFs\,L_{D}(t)\,L_{F} exceeds 1 across all (s,t)(s,t) we tested as shown in Fig. 32, so global contraction fails. Instead, we consider local convergence. Since Tt=Ds,t∘Rs∘FλT_{t}=D_{s,t}\circ R_{s}\circ F_{\lambda}, its local Lipschitz constant satisfies

LTtloc≤s​LDloc​(t)​LF.L_{T_{t}}^{\mathrm{loc}}\;\leq\;s\,L_{D}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t)\,L_{F}. (37)

While LF≤1L_{F}\leq 1, the denoiser constant LDloc​(t)L_{D}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t) typically increases with tt, reflecting the transition from an averaging (MMSE) estimator at t=st=s to a more mode-seeking estimator as t→1t\to 1. Consequently, the contraction factor degrades with tt, explaining the empirically observed loss of monotonic convergence for large lookaheads in Appendix C.7.

We assume there exists a closed neighborhood U⊂ℝdU\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} of a fixed point 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) such that Tt​(U)⊆UT_{t}(U)\subseteq U and

‖Tt​(𝐱)−Tt​(𝐱′)‖≤ρ⁡(t)​‖𝐱−𝐱′‖,∀𝐱,𝐱′∈U,\|T_{t}({\mathbf{x}})-T_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\|\leq\rho(t)\,\|{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}\|,\quad\forall{\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}\in U, (38)

with ρ⁡(t)≤s​LDloc​(t)​LF<1\rho(t)\leq s\,L_{D}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t)\,L_{F}<1. This local contraction assumption is standard in PnP (Ryu et al., 2019) and consistent with our empirical observations.

Theorem 2 (Local convergence to a lookahead-dependent fixed point)

Under (38), if the iteration enters UU, it converges geometrically to a unique fixed point 𝐱⋆​(t)∈U{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)\in U:

‖𝐱k−𝐱⋆​(t)‖≤ρ​(t)k​‖𝐱0−𝐱⋆​(t)‖.\|{\mathbf{x}}^{k}-{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)\|\leq\rho(t)^{k}\|{\mathbf{x}}^{0}-{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)\|. (39)

Moreover, 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) satisfies

𝐱⋆(t)=Ds,t(Rs(Fλ(𝐱⋆(t))))=Ds,t(s(𝐱⋆(t)−λ∇g(𝐱⋆(t)))),{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)=D_{s,t}\Bigl(R_{s}\bigl(F_{\lambda}({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t))\bigr)\Bigr)=D_{s,t}\bigl(s\,({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)-\lambda\nabla g({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)))\bigr),

so different lookaheads yield distinct fixed points whenever Ds,tD_{s,t} is genuinely tt-dependent.

The proof follows directly from the Banach fixed-point theorem applied to TtT_{t} on (U,∥⋅∥)(U,\|\cdot\|) and is given in Appendix D.4.1.

D.4.1 Proof of Theorem 2

Since UU is a closed subset of the complete metric space (ℝd,∥⋅∥)(\mathbb{R}^{d},\|\cdot\|), it is itself complete. By assumption, TtT_{t} maps UU into itself (Tt​(U)⊆UT_{t}(U)\subseteq U) and, by Equation 38, is a strict contraction on UU with constant ρ⁡(t)<1\rho(t)<1. The Banach fixed-point theorem then yields a unique 𝐱⋆​(t)∈U{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)\in U with Tt​(𝐱⋆​(t))=𝐱⋆​(t)T_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t))={\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t).

For the convergence rate, applying the contraction inequality with 𝐱′=𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}={\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) gives

‖𝐱k+1−𝐱⋆​(t)‖=‖Tt​(𝐱k)−Tt​(𝐱⋆​(t))‖≤ρ⁡(t)​‖𝐱k−𝐱⋆​(t)‖,\|{\mathbf{x}}^{k+1}-{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)\|=\|T_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{k})-T_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t))\|\leq\rho(t)\,\|{\mathbf{x}}^{k}-{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)\|,

and iterating yields the bound (39).

Finally, the fixed-point identity 𝐱⋆​(t)=Tt​(𝐱⋆​(t)){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)=T_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)) together with the operator definition (36) gives

𝐱⋆(t)=Ds,t(Rs(Fλ(𝐱⋆(t))))=Ds,t(s(𝐱⋆(t)−λ∇g(𝐱⋆(t)))),{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)=D_{s,t}\bigl(R_{s}(F_{\lambda}({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)))\bigr)=D_{s,t}\bigl(s\,({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)-\lambda\nabla g({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)))\bigr),

which depends on tt explicitly through Ds,tD_{s,t}. Whenever Ds,t≠Ds,t′D_{s,t}\neq D_{s,t^{\prime}} for t≠t′t\neq t^{\prime}, the corresponding fixed points 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) and 𝐱⋆​(t′){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t^{\prime}) differ.

Empirical Lipschitz analysis.

In Fig. 32, we plot the composite bound s​LD​(t)​LFs\,L_{D}(t)\,L_{F} for the deterministic PnP operator Tt=Ds,t∘Rs∘FλT_{t}=D_{s,t}\circ R_{s}\circ F_{\lambda} on CelebA 128×128128\times 128 (Gaussian kernel of size 4545, std 3.03.0, λ=1.0\lambda=1.0, giving LF=1.000L_{F}=1.000). The denoiser Lipschitz constant LD​(t)L_{D}(t) is estimated by alternating power iteration on the Jacobian of Ds,tD_{s,t} at noisy samples 𝐱s=s​𝐱1+(1−s)​ϵ{\mathbf{x}}_{s}=s\,{\mathbf{x}}_{1}+(1-s)\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, taking the worst case over 2020 samples. Across all (s,t)(s,t) tested, the bound exceeds 11 (red line), so TtT_{t} is never a global contraction; the algorithm’s empirical convergence is therefore explained by the local-contraction analysis of Theorem 2 rather than by a global Banach argument.

On the validation of assumption (38).

Empirical validation of (38) and the tt-dependence of fixed points is provided in the Gaussian linear-inverse setting (Appendix D.5.1, Fig. 33), where TtT_{t} admits a closed-form analysis and the iterates converge to the predicted Tikhonov solution to machine precision. For image priors, the deterministic operator analyzed in Theorem 2 is of theoretical interest; the algorithm deployed in practice (Algorithm 1) uses stochastic renoising, which both stabilizes the iteration and induces the variance restoration that drives the empirical distortion–perception behavior (Section 3.3).

D.5 Gaussian case: global contraction.

We now generalize the analysis from Section 3.2.1 (where the denoiser was treated as a standalone estimator without a forward model) to general linear inverse problems. Focusing on the multivariate case with a Gaussian prior p1=𝒩⁡(𝟎,σp2​𝐈)p_{1}={\mathcal{N}}(\mathbf{0},\,\sigma_{p}^{2}\,{\mathbf{I}}), the average denoiser remains a linear map Ds,t​(𝐱)=Λ⁡(s,t)​𝐱D_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})=\Lambda(s,t)\,{\mathbf{x}} with the same scalar gain (11). In this case, TtT_{t} is a global contraction and (38) holds with U=ℝdU=\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Since the denoiser gain is a scalar, LD​(t)=Λ⁡(s,t)L_{D}(t)=\Lambda(s,t) and LF=‖𝐈−λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇‖L_{F}=\|{\mathbf{I}}-\lambda\,{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}\|. The contraction rate is ρ⁡(t)=m⁡(t)​‖𝐈−λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇‖\rho(t)=m(t)\,\|{\mathbf{I}}-\lambda\,{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}\|, where m⁡(t):=s​Λ​(s,t)<1m(t):=s\,\Lambda(s,t)<1 for all t∈[s,1]t\in[s,1] and s∈(0,1)s\in(0,1) (Appendix D.2). For any λ∈(0, 2/‖𝐇⊤​𝐇‖)\lambda\in(0,\,2/\|{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}\|), we have ‖𝐈−λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇‖≤1\|{\mathbf{I}}-\lambda\,{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}\|\leq 1. Consequently, ρ⁡(t)<1\rho(t)<1 on all of [s,1][s,1]: the Gaussian case admits unconditional global convergence across all lookaheads, even for ill-posed forward models. Solving the fixed-point equation yields the closed form

𝐱⋆​(t)=(c⁡(t)​𝐈+λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇)−1​λ​𝐇⊤​𝐲,c⁡(t)=1m⁡(t)−1,{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)\;=\;\bigl(c(t)\,{\mathbf{I}}+\lambda\,{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}\bigr)^{-1}\,\lambda\,{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}},\qquad c(t)\;=\;\frac{1}{m(t)}-1, (40)

i.e., a Tikhonov-regularized estimator whose regularization parameter c⁡(t)c(t) depends on both the forward model 𝐇{\mathbf{H}} and the lookahead tt. Since Λ⁡(s,t)\Lambda(s,t) is strictly increasing in tt (Appendix D.2), c⁡(t)c(t) is strictly decreasing. As the lookahead increases from ss to 11, the Tikhonov regularization progressively weakens, yielding a continuum of estimators with decreasing shrinkage toward the prior mean. In contrast to the denoising setting, these fixed points do not, in general, correspond to the MMSE or lie on the optimal distortion–perception frontier; instead, the lookahead acts as a regularization parameter that controls the bias–variance trade-off of the reconstruction.

D.5.1 Proof of Equation (40): Fixed Point for the Gaussian Case

By definition, the fixed point 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) satisfies 𝐱⋆​(t)=Tt​(𝐱⋆​(t)){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)=T_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)). For a linear inverse problem with data fidelity g⁡(𝐱)=12​‖𝐇𝐱−𝐲‖2g({\mathbf{x}})=\frac{1}{2}\|{\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}\|^{2}, the gradient is ∇g​(𝐱)=𝐇⊤​(𝐇𝐱−𝐲)\nabla g({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{H}}^{\top}({\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}). The gradient descent step is given by:

Fλ​(𝐱)=s⁡(𝐱−λ​𝐇⊤​(𝐇𝐱−𝐲)).F_{\lambda}({\mathbf{x}})=s\bigl({\mathbf{x}}-\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}({\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}})\bigr).

In the multivariate Gaussian case, the average denoiser is the linear map Ds,t​(𝐱)=Λ⁡(s,t)​𝐱D_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})=\Lambda(s,t){\mathbf{x}}. Substituting this into the fixed-point equation yields:

𝐱⋆​(t)\displaystyle{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) =Ds,t​(Fλ​(𝐱⋆​(t)))\displaystyle=D_{s,t}\bigl(F_{\lambda}({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t))\bigr)
𝐱⋆​(t)\displaystyle{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) =Λ⁡(s,t)⋅s⁡(𝐱⋆​(t)−λ​𝐇⊤​(𝐇𝐱⋆​(t)−𝐲)).\displaystyle=\Lambda(s,t)\cdot s\bigl({\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)-\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}({\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)-{\mathbf{y}})\bigr).

Defining the effective scaling factor m⁡(t):=s​Λ​(s,t)m(t):=s\,\Lambda(s,t), we can distribute m⁡(t)m(t) across the terms:

𝐱⋆​(t)=m⁡(t)​𝐱⋆​(t)−m⁡(t)​λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇𝐱⋆​(t)+m⁡(t)​λ​𝐇⊤​𝐲.{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)=m(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)-m(t)\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)+m(t)\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}.

Since m⁡(t)∈(0,1)m(t)\in(0,1) across all valid lookaheads t∈[s,1]t\in[s,1] (as shown in Appendix D.2), it is strictly positive. We can therefore divide both sides by m⁡(t)m(t):

1m⁡(t)​𝐱⋆​(t)=𝐱⋆​(t)−λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇𝐱⋆​(t)+λ​𝐇⊤​𝐲.\frac{1}{m(t)}{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)={\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)-\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)+\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}.

Subtracting 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) from both sides and rearranging to group all terms involving 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) on the left yields:

(1m⁡(t)−1)​𝐱⋆​(t)+λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇𝐱⋆​(t)=λ​𝐇⊤​𝐲.\left(\frac{1}{m(t)}-1\right){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)+\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)=\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}.

Factoring out 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) gives:

[(1m⁡(t)−1)​𝐈+λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇]​𝐱⋆​(t)=λ​𝐇⊤​𝐲.\biggl[\left(\frac{1}{m(t)}-1\right){\mathbf{I}}+\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}\biggr]{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)=\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}.

Finally, defining the regularization parameter as c⁡(t):=1m⁡(t)−1c(t):=\frac{1}{m(t)}-1, we invert the matrix on the left-hand side to arrive at the closed-form solution:

𝐱⋆​(t)=(c⁡(t)​𝐈+λ​𝐇⊤​𝐇)−1​λ​𝐇⊤​𝐲,{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)=\bigl(c(t){\mathbf{I}}+\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}\bigr)^{-1}\lambda{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}},

which completes the derivation.

Empirical validation.

To corroborate the closed form (40), we consider a 2D Gaussian prior p1=𝒩⁡(𝟎,σp2​𝐈)p_{1}={\mathcal{N}}(\mathbf{0},\sigma_{p}^{2}\,{\mathbf{I}}) with σp=2\sigma_{p}=2, and two linear forward models: an isotropic rotation 𝐇1=0.8​R​(π/6){\mathbf{H}}_{1}=0.8\,R(\pi/6) and an anisotropic operator 𝐇2=R⁡(π/6)​diag​(1.0, 0.3)​R​(π/4){\mathbf{H}}_{2}=R(\pi/6)\,\mathrm{diag}(1.0,\,0.3)\,R(\pi/4), whose Gram matrix 𝐇2⊤​𝐇2{\mathbf{H}}_{2}^{\top}{\mathbf{H}}_{2} has eigenvalues {1.0, 0.09}\{1.0,\,0.09\} and couples the coordinates. Observations are 𝐲=𝐇k​𝐱1+η{\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{H}}_{k}\,{\mathbf{x}}_{1}+\eta with η∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,σobs2​𝐈)\eta\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mathbf{0},\sigma_{\rm obs}^{2}\,{\mathbf{I}}), σobs=0.1\sigma_{\rm obs}=0.1.

We run deterministic PnP-Flow (ϵ=0\epsilon=0) with λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 and 0.50.5, anchor s=0.45s=0.45, and lookaheads t∈{s,s+0.27, 1}t\in\{s,\,s+0.27,\,1\}. The iterates converge to 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) to machine precision (‖𝐱^−𝐱⋆​(t)‖mean<5⋅10−16\|\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}-{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t)\|_{\rm mean}<5\cdot 10^{-16}), validating (40). As tt increases, the effective regularization c⁡(t)/λc(t)/\lambda decreases (0.93→0.59→0.430.93\to 0.59\to 0.43), yielding a continuum of Tikhonov estimators with progressively weaker shrinkage toward the prior mean. The result is shown in Fig. 33

In this Gaussian inverse problem, the lookahead acts as a regularization knob rather than a parameterization of the distortion–perception frontier. Since the regime is strongly over-regularized, increasing tt reduces bias and decreases the empirical MSE. This does not contradict the image experiments: exact distortion–perception optimality holds only in the denoising setting, while in inverse problems the interaction with the forward model breaks this guarantee. Here, the Gaussian case isolates the algorithmic role of the lookahead through its closed-form Tikhonov interpretation. This highlights that the exact DP interpretation holds in the denoising setting, while in inverse problems the lookahead acts as a forward-model-dependent regularization parameter.

Why 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) is not the MAP/Wiener estimator.

One might expect PnP with Ds,t=sD_{s,t=s} (the MMSE denoiser) to recover the MAP estimator 𝐱MAP{\mathbf{x}}_{\rm MAP}, as in classical PnP with proximal operators. This is not the case. The flow-map denoiser Ds,t​(𝐱)=Λ⁡(s,t)​𝐱D_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})=\Lambda(s,t)\,{\mathbf{x}} is not a proximal map: it operates at the intrinsic noise level σs\sigma_{s} of the interpolant 𝐱s{\mathbf{x}}_{s}, rather than the measurement noise σobs\sigma_{\rm obs}.

Matching (40) to 𝐱MAP{\mathbf{x}}_{\rm MAP} would require c⁡(t)/λ=σobs2/σp2c(t)/\lambda=\sigma_{\rm obs}^{2}/\sigma_{p}^{2}, which is incompatible with the contraction regime. Consequently, PnP-Flow operates at an effectively higher noise level, yielding over-regularized estimates. As the lookahead tt increases, c⁡(t)c(t) decreases and 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) moves toward the Wiener solution, reducing bias. Thus, the lookahead controls a bias–variance trade-off induced by this noise mismatch, rather than traversing the optimal distortion–perception curve. In general, 𝐱⋆​(t){\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) should be interpreted as a lookahead-controlled Tikhonov estimator.

Effect of renoising in the Gaussian setting.

To isolate the role of the renoising step, we repeat the experiment with the full stochastic PnP iteration. While the deterministic case converges to a single Tikhonov solution, the stochastic iteration produces a distribution of estimates whose spread is largely independent of the step size λ\lambda.

Across different λ\lambda, the sample clouds consistently exhibit meaningful variance and align with the geometry of the data distribution, even when the mean estimate remains over-regularized. This indicates that the renoising step, together with the denoiser, primarily controls the variance of the estimator, while λ\lambda governs its mean through the data-consistency update.

As the lookahead increases, this variability is progressively amplified, yielding the distortion–perception behavior observed in the experiment.
